incumbent

in-KUM-bunt · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Incumbent means the person currently holding a particular office or position of authority.

The incumbent campaigned from the comfort of the office she already held, while three challengers scrambled just to get their names noticed.

Example

When the raiders launched their hostile takeover, the incumbent chief executive refused to step aside, reminding the board that she—not some outside investor—had run the firm for the past nine years.

Notice that "incumbent" points to the person who currently holds the position—here, the chief executive who is already in charge and is now defending her seat against an outside raid. This is different from a candidate or a nominee. A candidate is merely someone running for or seeking a position, and a nominee is someone proposed for one; neither of them necessarily holds it yet. The incumbent is defined precisely by already being in the role. So the investor trying to seize control is a challenger or would-be successor, never the incumbent—no matter how much power he manages to grab—until he actually takes the office.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

officeholder: An officeholder is anyone formally holding an office right now — the most neutral single word. Incumbent means the same current occupant but carries a built-in contrast with rivals who want the seat, which is why election coverage says incumbent rather than officeholder.

sitting official: Sitting official describes someone presently serving, with 'sitting' doing the same work incumbent does. But the phrase leans on a title — a sitting judge, a sitting president — while incumbent stands alone as a noun and adds the sense of a position being defended.

current holder: Current holder is the plain, flexible paraphrase for whoever occupies a position at the moment, from a job to a world record. Incumbent is the formal, political word for the same person, at home in elections, appointments, and contests for the seat.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

successor: The person who takes over the position afterward — the future occupant, where the incumbent is the present one.

challenger: A person actively trying to take the office away from its current holder — the incumbent's direct opposite in any election or contest.

Where it sits · how fully the office is one's own

contender → acting holder → incumbent

contender vs. incumbent: A contender is still only campaigning for the seat, while the incumbent already occupies it — the whole contest is between wanting the office and holding it.

acting holder vs. incumbent: An acting holder fills the chair temporarily, as a caretaker, but the incumbent possesses the office in full, having been elected or appointed to it in her own right.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — in-: upon, on (Latin)

Root — -cumb-: to lie down (Latin -cumbere, a nasalized form of cubare, "to lie")

Suffix — -ent: one who; forms nouns and adjectives from verbs

Put it together: Latin incumbere meant "to lie down upon, lean on" — in- ("upon") plus -cumbere ("to lie down," a nasalized form of cubare). Add -ent ("one who") and an incumbent is literally "one lying upon" something — in English, the person settled into an office, occupying the seat. The picture is vivid: while challengers stand outside campaigning, the incumbent is the one already reclining in the chair. The same lying-down root gives recumbent (leaning back or lying down) and succumb (literally "to lie down under" a pressure — to give in to it).

Use the root in a new word: recumbent: The stone knight lies recumbent atop his tomb — literally "lying back," from the same Latin root as incumbent.

Strength Check

Word Choice

formal / political / institutional

"incumbent" (as a noun for the current officeholder) is a formal word at home in political, corporate, legal, and journalistic writing—elections, board seats, church appointments, and the like. In casual conversation you'd more likely say "the person currently in charge" or name the office directly.
